{"id": "24:21/q15", "question": "What does lawlā contribute grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "24:21/q15/p1", "position": "Here it is an exception-preventing particle followed by a nominal clause; a positive answer takes lām and a negative answer does not.", "reasons": "Itqān adds that a following pronoun should be nominative. It also records lawlā as halā for exhortation or offer and as rebuke or regret elsewhere; al-Harawī's suggested interrogative examples are better read as halā. The majority reject al-Harawī's negation analysis of another verse, supported by Ubayy's halā reading."}]}
{"id": "24:21/q16", "question": "Why is favor and mercy repeated?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "24:21/q16/p1", "position": "The repetition recalls delayed punishment and emphasizes the gravity of the slander and dependence on God.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā refers to the earlier explanation at 24:20; Zamakhsharī notes repeated omitted answers, Bayḍāwī the delayed punishment, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī the now explicit answer about purification. Asad sends readers to 24:10 and its note."}]}
{"id": "24:21/q17", "question": "Whom does 'none of you' concern?", "turns_on": "Whether the statement is universal or locally addressed to the people implicated in the slander.", "positions": [{"id": "24:21/q17/p1", "position": "All people or all the addressees: none could be guided or made righteous unaided.", "reasons": "Ahl al-maʿānī and some exegetes give the general reading. Ibn ʿAbbās says no one can secure good or avert harm alone; Ṭabrisī mentions Satan's whispering. Ibn ʿĀshūr connects it to the danger of Satan's trial; Kuranyolu names ego and Satan as life's obstacles."}, {"id": "24:21/q17/p2", "position": "It particularly concerns those who took part in the slander; none would be cleansed of that offense without accepted repentance.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās via ʿAṭāʾ says their repentance would not have been accepted; Wāḥidī explains repair after their sin. Baghawī reports this group, while Nasafī stresses expiatory repentance and Wāḥidī's Wajīz specifies forgiveness."}]}
{"id": "24:21/q18", "question": "What does zakā mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the outcome is described as cleansing, moral soundness, or guidance and Islam.", "positions": [{"id": "24:21/q18/p1", "position": "To become pure or cleansed from sin.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba gives purity; Ṭabarī specifies sins and shirk; Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī the stain of sin. Rāzī likens a zakī person's attained obedience to a mature crop; one is called pure only when truly so. Biqāʿī includes growth in the word's sense."}, {"id": "24:21/q18/p2", "position": "To become sound, upright or righteous.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Abū Zayd give soundness; Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Q and later summaries use ṣāliḥ."}, {"id": "24:21/q18/p3", "position": "To be guided, enter Islam or recognize right guidance.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd generalizes that every Qurʾanic zakā or tazakkā means Islam; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Qurṭubī associate this sense with the majority's light reading. Study Quran reports guidance and Islam separately."}]}
{"id": "24:21/q19", "question": "How is mā zakā read?", "turns_on": "Gemination of kāf and treatment of the final alif; transmitted reader lists and imāla vary.", "positions": [{"id": "24:21/q19/p1", "position": "A light kāf, the common reading, with the verb describing becoming pure or guided.", "reasons": "Jishumī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya explain the sense; Samīn derives it from zakā yazkū and records imāla or its absence on the final alif. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the familiar reading has no imāla; Abu Ḥayyān reports that some do apply it. Ibn Mujāhid names Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī among forms left without imāla."}, {"id": "24:21/q19/p2", "position": "A doubled kāf, mā zakkā, making purification God's action on the person.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī cites the later yuzakkī in support and names Ibn Muḥayṣin and Yaʿqūb; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Qurṭubī name Abū Ḥaywa and al-Ḥasan; Samīn names al-Aʿmash and Abū Jaʿfar. Ālūsī reports gemination with imāla from Rūḥ and al-Aʿmash. The reader lists vary."}, {"id": "24:21/q19/p3", "position": "An imāla of the alif is transmitted.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinnī names Abū Jaʿfar, Shayba, two ʿĪsās, and reports from ʿĀṣim and al-Aʿmash. He explains that imāla is a kind of inflection and verbs admit it more readily than nouns, contrasting al-ʿafā and al-sanā; reports differ on whether this accompanies gemination."}]}
{"id": "24:21/q20", "question": "Why is zakā written with a yāʾ-shaped alif?", "turns_on": "Whether the written yāʾ shape is explained by imāla or analogy, or treated as orthography independent of oral transmission.", "positions": [{"id": "24:21/q20/p1", "position": "The spelling can reflect imāla or analogy with the doubled form despite the wāw root.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinnī derives the verb from zakawtu yazkū and uses that to account for imāla; Samīn and Ālūsī offer imāla or the doubled reading for the orthography, the latter citing Abū Ḥayyān."}, {"id": "24:21/q20/p2", "position": "The expected spelling is plain alif, but the muṣḥaf's yāʾ shape does not change the spoken reading.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the familiar light verb has a wāw root and no imāla; transmission safeguards pronunciation, and only altering pronounced letters would conflict with the muṣḥaf."}]}
{"id": "24:21/q21", "question": "How are minkum min aḥadin parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "24:21/q21/p1", "position": "The first min explains the group; the second is extra for emphasis, and aḥad is the subject with light zakā or object with doubled zakkā.", "reasons": "Bursevī gives the subject parse; Samīn and Ālūsī contrast both readings and make God the subject of doubled zakkā. Biqāʿī says repeated min excludes every single person."}]}
{"id": "24:21/q22", "question": "What force does abadan have?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "24:21/q22/p1", "position": "It extends the denial through all time, without an endpoint.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī connects it with emphatic min, while Bursevī and Ālūsī gloss it as forever."}]}
{"id": "24:21/q23", "question": "How does God purify whom He wills?", "turns_on": "Whether purification is stated as divine making-righteous, specified through repentance, or conditioned on preparedness and a request.", "positions": [{"id": "24:21/q23/p1", "position": "He makes the chosen person pure or righteous by grace.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Yaḥyā, Saʿīd and al-Kalbī give righteousness; Ibn Qutayba gives purification. Ṭabrisī describes favor that makes a person righteous before God. Ibn Kathīr adds different degrees of removal of shirk, immorality and bad traits, and divine choice in guidance or misguidance; Biqāʿī mentions soul and heart diseases and protection from the slander. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says good works reveal prior destiny for felicity."}, {"id": "24:21/q23/p2", "position": "He guides people to repentance and accepts it, cleansing their sins.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī relates Ibn ʿAbbās's will to accept the slanderers' repentance; Nasafī specifies sincere repentance. Bayḍāwī, Bursevī and Ālūsī include both enabling and accepting repentance, the last limiting the slanderers to those free of hypocrisy. Abū Ḥayyān allows this alongside prior felicity."}, {"id": "24:21/q23/p3", "position": "He purifies those prepared for it who request it through their state of readiness.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says God hears their request and knows their preparedness."}]}
{"id": "24:21/q24", "question": "Does divine purification create a person's purity or describe grace and judgment?", "turns_on": "Whether tazkiya means producing purity, providing enabling grace, or judging purity, and how divine will relates to evil acts.", "positions": [{"id": "24:21/q24/p1", "position": "God produces purity in the person; purification depends on His will and enabling.", "reasons": "Rāzī's school compares tazkiya to making something black or red. Rāzī says the verse explicitly supports its account; the will clause and 'favor and mercy' make purification discretionary. Bursevī says the verse refutes Qadariyya claims of purification through worship alone. Ibn ʿAṭiyya treats deeds as signs of prior felicity."}, {"id": "24:21/q24/p2", "position": "God performs gracious acts, luṭf, that help the servant become pure.", "reasons": "Rāzī attributes this to Muʿtazilites, then argues: ineffectual luṭf is irrelevant; an impossible effect deters, a merely possible effect lacks a determinant, and a necessary effect makes God creator of the act. He adds that obligatory luṭf cannot be the contingent favor and mercy described here."}, {"id": "24:21/q24/p3", "position": "God judges or declares that a servant is pure.", "reasons": "Rāzī attributes this second interpretation to Muʿtazilites and objects that God must declare the truth and cannot make it depend on will without falsehood."}, {"id": "24:21/q24/p4", "position": "God does not will the indecency Satan wills; He acts for morally responsible people's good.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī argues that if God created and willed the indecency He condemns, He would merit greater blame than its commander, which is impossible for Him; His hearing and knowledge inform beneficial action."}]}
{"id": "24:21/q25", "question": "What spiritual means help a person receive purification?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "24:21/q25/p1", "position": "God enables obedience by grace, while a teacher or spiritual guide helps a seeker learn purification.", "reasons": "Bursevī calls the Prophet the greatest means; ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī credits Abū al-Ḥasan al-Kharaqānī rather than his many hadith and law teachers for teaching him the spiritual path. Guides and the perfected person's companionship open certainty."}]}

Ṭabāṭabāʾī applies hearing to the request for purification and knowledge to readiness."}]}
{"id": "24:21/q27", "question": "Why repeat God's name in the closing statement?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "24:21/q27/p1", "position": "The explicit divine name reinforces hearing and knowledge and gives the close the force of an independent maxim.", "reasons": "Ālūsī says the repeated name evokes divinity and urges sincere repentance; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the sentence stands like a proverb."}]}
{"id": "24:21/q28", "question": "How does this warning relate to the slander passage and other verses?", "turns_on": "Whether the connection is to the immediate slander narrative or wider parallel teachings; both may apply.", "positions": [{"id": "24:21/q28/p1", "position": "It identifies slander, credulous rumor-spreading and desire for scandal as Satan's path in the surrounding account.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr places it after ten slander verses; Iṣlāḥī locates 11–26 in the hypocrites' false accusation campaign and says some Muslims unwittingly amplified it. He connects the warning with the preceding directive and demands proof before relaying claims. Study Quran names the false accusation against ʿĀʾisha and community response. Asad warns accusers against forgetting human weakness."}, {"id": "24:21/q28/p2", "position": "The verse's warning parallels other Qurʾanic statements about Satan and divine goodness.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān points to 2:168, Ṭabāṭabāʾī to 2:208, Study Quran to 2:168, 2:208, 6:142, 2:169 and 2:268; Ṭabāṭabāʾī links divine goodness with 3:26, 4:79 and 11:108. Ibn ʿĀshūr compares faḥshāʾ with 2:169 and munkar with 3:104."}]}
{"id": "24:21/q29", "question": "What does this passage teach about willing or loving grave sin?", "turns_on": "The moral weight assigned to a resolve compared with the intended act.", "positions": [{"id": "24:21/q29/p1", "position": "Inward love, intention or approval can itself incur blame; willing disbelief is disbelief.", "reasons": "Jishumī infers accountability from the threat attached to love and reports agreement that intending, desiring, approving or loving disbelief counts as disbelief, all being acts of the heart."}, {"id": "24:21/q29/p2", "position": "Resolving to commit a grave sin is as grave as the intended deed.", "reasons": "Jishumī attributes this to Abū ʿAlī."}, {"id": "24:21/q29/p3", "position": "Resolve is less grave than the intended sin, although it can itself become grave.", "reasons": "Jishumī attributes this to Abū Hāshim."}]}
{"id": "24:21/q30", "question": "Do legal penalties expiate the sins they punish?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "24:21/q30/p1", "position": "Prescribed penalties can expiate sins, except apostasy according to one group.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī and Bursevī count these penalties among God's favor. Ālūsī reports a group's exclusion of apostasy and says they answer an earlier Abū Hurayra report by dating it before revelation of this rule."}]}
{"id": "24:21/q31", "question": "What conduct does the warning call for?", "turns_on": "The notes offer complementary practical counsels.", "positions": [{"id": "24:21/q31/p1", "position": "Reject rumors and unfounded accusations; repent sincerely and guard one's speech.", "reasons": "Abū al-Dardāʾ reports the Prophet's warnings against partisanship without knowledge, thwarting a divine limit and falsely damaging a Muslim, tying these to 24:19. Bursevī cites hadith that speech usually counts against its speaker, lying to a trusting brother is treachery, and one's own faults should occupy one. Ālūsī urges sincerity in repentance; Iṣlāḥī requires investigation."}, {"id": "24:21/q31/p2", "position": "Support purification through lawful livelihood and wise company while avoiding sinful company.", "reasons": "Bursevī advises lawful spending, the company of jurists and the wise, and avoidance of the ignorant and sinful."}]}
{"id": "24:36/q01", "question": "How does “in houses” connect syntactically to the surrounding verses?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase completes the lamp parable, introduces the worshippers, or resumes an earlier passage; the chosen reading of يسبح and the pause at 24:35 also matter.", "positions": [{"id": "24:36/q01/p1", "position": "It qualifies the niche, lamp, glass, or their location in the preceding light parable.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj, Abū Ḥātim, al-Wāḥidī, al-Samīn and others offer the link to مشكاة or مصباح; al-Samīn also lists زجاجة. This keeps the parable continuous and locates its exemplar in worship houses. Ibn ʿĀshūr says these are generic nouns; Biqāʿī likewise treats the singular fittings as a type. Rāzī notes many investigators supply the implied niche; Kur’an Yolu summarizes the possible antecedents."}, {"id": "24:36/q01/p2", "position": "It attaches to the preceding verb for kindling: the lamp is lit in houses.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī permits attachment to تُوقَد; al-Rummānī and later grammarians state this parse. Ibn ʿĀshūr notes it locates the lamp, while al-Bayḍāwī says it gives the example a fine setting."}, {"id": "24:36/q01/p3", "position": "It attaches forward to يسبح, with فيها repeated for emphasis: worshippers glorify God in these houses.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Farrāʾ, al-Wāḥidī and others accept fronting; Rāzī defends repetition as preferable to ellipsis. Al-Samīn cites 11:108; al-Ālūsī says fronting signals importance rather than exclusivity; Ibn ʿĀshūr says it raises anticipation. The pause at عليم is possible. Al-Khafājī disputes al-Ālūsī's interruption objection, locating the parable's end earlier; al-Samīn corrects an enumeration of parses."}, {"id": "24:36/q01/p4", "position": "A fresh sentence supplies an omitted command or verb, such as “pray” or “glorify in houses.”", "reasons": "Al-Jubbāʾī supplies a command to pray; al-Kashshāf and al-Samīn cite 27:12 for an omitted verb. Al-Wāḥidī favors a fresh description because plural houses do not extend the singular niche; the pause at عليم follows."}, {"id": "24:36/q01/p5", "position": "It reaches back to the examples of earlier people in 24:34, understood as prophets and righteous people whose houses were mosques.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim cites prophetic prayer chambers, including the intruders in 38:21; he says intervening text does not bar return to the earlier topic. Al-Qāḍī objects that 24:34 concerns deniers and slave-girl coercion and that 24:35 intervenes."}, {"id": "24:36/q01/p6", "position": "It is a settled circumstantial phrase modifying “His light” in the preceding verse, portraying Qur’an received and studied in gatherings.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers this reading, supported by the report on people gathering in a house of God for recitation and study."}, {"id": "24:36/q01/p7", "position": "It is a fronted predicate with “men” as subject, answering who receives the preceding light.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr offers this as another possible fresh construction. Al-Wāḥidī says the passive reading prevents forward attachment to يسبح, an argument for a fresh parse."}, {"id": "24:36/q01/p8", "position": "It attaches to “His name be remembered” as an adverbial expression.", "reasons": "Kur’an Yolu states this; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Samīn reject direct attachment because يذكر is within أن and cannot govern a preceding phrase."}, {"id": "24:36/q01/p9", "position": "It begins a statement placing God in the houses.", "reasons": "Al-Tirmidhī al-Ḥakīm cites a report on a mosque sitter being in the company of his Lord and a Torah report about divine hospitality."}]}
{"id": "24:36/q02", "question": "How can a singular niche and lamp appear in plural houses?", "turns_on": "Whether the parable depicts an individual object, a generic type, or a shift in address.", "positions": [{"id": "24:36/q02/p1", "position": "The singular denotes a type, with an instance in each house.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says matching lamps illuminate each worship house at night; al-Bayḍāwī and Ibn ʿĀshūr call the objects generic; al-Biqāʿī says the singular fittings convey the light's rarity."}, {"id": "24:36/q02/p2", "position": "It is a shift from singular to plural address.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī cites 33:1; al-Qurṭubī cites 65:1."}, {"id": "24:36/q02/p3", "position": "A plural setting can contain a singular object in one member, just as the moon is said to be in the heavens.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Qurṭubī cite 71:16."}, {"id": "24:36/q02/p4", "position": "The mismatch is an objection to placing the lamp in the houses.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim says one lamp cannot occupy every house; he also says a mosque setting adds no brightness. Rāzī counters that the glass lamp in a mosque is grander and completes the parable."}]}
{"id": "24:36/q03", "question": "What does بُيُوتٍ mean as an Arabic word?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "24:36/q03/p1", "position": "It means dwellings or places in which something resides.", "reasons": "Al-Rāghib says bayt originally designated a person's night dwelling, then any dwelling; buyūt is for houses, abyāt for poetry, and the word can extend to any locus."}]}
{"id": "24:36/q04", "question": "How is the first consonant of بُيُوتٍ read?", "turns_on": "The variant is dialectal and has no difference of sense.", "positions": [{"id": "24:36/q04/p1", "position": "With ḍamma on the bāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī report this alongside kasra."}, {"id": "24:36/q04/p2", "position": "With kasra on the bāʾ.", "reasons": "Qirāʾāt Encyclopedia calls it dialectal, without semantic change."}]}

He says God inspired the builders and permitted the structures' worship purpose, with 22:40 and 57:27 as parallels."}, {"id": "24:36/q05/p9", "position": "Jerusalem's churches, or earlier scriptural worship buildings.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr records Jerusalem churches; Kur’an Yolu adds synagogues as places with lamps and non-idolatrous worship."}, {"id": "24:36/q05/p10", "position": "Primarily directly commanded worship sites, the Kaʿba and Jerusalem sanctuary, with their branches.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī excludes idolatrous shrines as impure."}, {"id": "24:36/q05/p11", "position": "The worshipper's inner stations or heart.", "reasons": "Qāshānī identifies stages of soul, heart, secret and spirit; Qushayrī calls hearts houses of gnosis. {"id": "24:36/q06", "question": "What does God’s أَذِنَ convey here?", "turns_on": "Whether permission is command, mere allowance and enablement, or inspiration.", "positions": [{"id": "24:36/q06/p1", "position": "God commanded or decreed it.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Kashshāf, al-Qurṭubī and others give command; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī add that the root includes knowledge and enabling without prohibition. Al-Ālūsī says calling command permission suggests an already eager addressee."}, {"id": "24:36/q06/p2", "position": "God made it permissible, informed people of that permission, and enabled it.", "reasons": "Bursevī defines izin as granting leave; Biqāʿī includes permission, enablement, recommendation and obligation."}, {"id": "24:36/q06/p3", "position": "God inspired builders to erect them for worship.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says monasteries were not commanded in original Christianity but were not forbidden, and good intent made their construction pleasing to God; he cites 22:40 and 57:27."}]}
{"id": "24:36/q07", "question": "What does it mean for the houses to be raised?", "turns_on": "Whether رُفع is physical building or spiritual honor, and whether the wording presupposes existing buildings.", "positions": [{"id": "24:36/q07/p1", "position": "They are built or physically elevated.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and others compare Abraham raising the House's foundations in 2:127; al-Kashshāf adds 79:28. Al-Ṭabarī prefers common architectural usage.
